mechanism: For qualifying large distributions, FINRA Rule 11140 can move the ex-date to the first business day after the payable date. During the resulting due-bill period, a seller who is record-holder can still owe the distribution to a purchaser, so the economic entitlement follows the security through a post-record-date trading window rather than the record date alone. Issuer/exchange notices can also create a when-issued or ex-distribution line that separates entitlement-bearing and non-entitlement-bearing claims. The candidate mechanism is a settlement-entitlement/operational-attention dislocation, not a dividend-yield signal.
claim: A mechanically identifiable subset of large cash or stock distributions creates an unusual public entitlement clock in which due bills transfer the distribution to buyers until the delayed ex-date. A future frozen test may ask whether entitlement-bearing and non-entitlement-bearing claims are ever priced inconsistently with the contractual distribution after costs and settlement constraints. No pricing inefficiency or positive return is claimed here.
prediction: Before any price or return data are opened, every admissible event must have primary evidence for the distribution amount/type, record date, payable date, ex-date and due-bill rule or exchange announcement. If an entitlement-separated when-issued/ex-distribution line exists, its exact symbol/CUSIP/trading window must also be frozen. The structural prediction is only that trade-date entitlement differs from a naive record-date interpretation; economic mispricing remains unknown.
falsification_scope: Kill this mechanism as a testable event/document candidate if current rule/application does not create an entitlement-transfer period for the selected class of events, if issuer/exchange notices do not provide a point-in-time clock sufficient to determine entitlement before trading, or if settlement/corporate-action processing makes the theoretical entitlement non-executable for a small account. A later absence of price dislocation falsifies only the frozen economic expression, not the due-bill legal mechanics.

decision_map.source_clock: Earliest primary issuer/regulatory/exchange publication that definitively states the distribution and entitlement dates; later exchange updates may amend amount/date fields but cannot retroactively define an earlier signal.
decision_map.event_definition: Distribution for which the applicable regulatory/exchange treatment explicitly delays the ex-date past the payable date or explicitly establishes a due-bill period transferring entitlement through trades. Do not infer eligibility solely from distribution size unless the governing notice/rule application is verified.
admissibility: Primary issuer, FINRA or listing-exchange document available before any candidate price observation
Record date, payable date and ex-date stated or mechanically derivable from the controlling notice
Due-bill entitlement transfer is explicit for the event or directly controlled by the cited rule
Security/CUSIP and any when-issued or ex-distribution symbol are unambiguous
No outcome, return or post-event price is used to select the event
decision_map.payer: Any potential rent would come from counterparties mispricing entitlement, operationally constrained holders, or liquidity demand during the due-bill window; the issuer's distribution itself is not free alpha.
decision_map.capacity_intuition: Event-specific and likely small. Large distributions can attract arbitrageurs, while borrow, settlement, tax, corporate-action processing and the short entitlement window constrain capacity and may erase any spread.
fatal_risks: The distribution is already perfectly capitalized in both ordinary and when-issued prices
Borrow or short-sale treatment transfers due bills cleanly and eliminates naive arbitrage
Broker/custodian handling, withholding tax or corporate-action fees differ from theoretical entitlement
When-issued liquidity is too thin or unavailable to the target account
Rule treatment varies by security type or venue, so a broad >=25% heuristic would be invalid

primary_documentary_evidence.fact: For dividends/distributions at least 25% of security value, the ex-date is the first business day following the payable date; a seller before that ex-date may have to relinquish the distribution to the buyer.
Issuer explains that because its special dividend exceeded 25% of trading price, Nasdaq advised a due-bill period; purchasers during that period receive the cash dividend and sellers do not.
Current example publishes record, payment, ex and due-bill redemption dates and a separate THRMV when-issued line explicitly not entitled to the special cash dividend. No price data were used.

nearby_but_distinct: ETF liquidation NAV convergence converts fund shares to liquidation value; this candidate concerns trade-date distribution entitlement before ex-date
reverse-split cash-in-lieu/round-up concerns fractional shares, not due-bill transfer of distributions
SPAC redemption and odd-lot tender protocols concern issuer redemption/tender rights, not delayed ex-date entitlement
month-end pension rebalance is broad institutional flow, not event-specific settlement entitlement

next_validator_decision.PASS_TO_TEST_DESIGN: Rule applicability and at least one event can be frozen from primary documents with exact entitlement clock and instrument mapping before any price observation.
next_validator_decision.PARK_DATA: Legal mechanics are real but current event identification, when-issued mapping, broker entitlement semantics or PIT source availability cannot support a clean test.
next_validator_decision.KILL_MECHANISM: The supposed due-bill transfer does not create a separately testable entitlement state after accounting for actual exchange/settlement rules.
